original_poem:
چاند سے مکھڑا

چاند سے مکھڑا تیری آنکھوں کا جادو
دیکھوں تو جھک جائے یہ میری نگاہوں کا جادو

ساری دنیا کا رنگ دیکھوں
پھر بھی مجھے تیرے چہرے کی روشنی میں سجدہ ہے

گزرے پل کے گزر جانے کا دکھ بھی
ہنس کر بھی میرے دل کی دھڑکنوں میں ہوتا ہے

چاہت کا یہ جادو، محبت کا یہ جال
چاند سے مکھڑے کی گود میں سجے رہیں گے
translated_poem:
Face Like the Moon

Your face, like the moon,
Holds the magic of your eyes,
When I gaze, this magic
Makes my sight bow low.

I see the colors of the world,
Yet, I bow in the light of your face.

The sorrow of passing moments
Also becomes a joy, as
I smile through the beating of my heart.

This magic of love, this web of affection,
Will always be adorned in the lap of your face like the moon.

source_lines: چاند سے مکھڑا تیری آنکھوں کا جادو
دیکھوں تو جھک جائے یہ میری نگاہوں کا جادو
translated_lines: Your face, like the moon,
Holds the magic of your eyes,
When I gaze, this magic
Makes my sight bow low.
stanzas.loss_note: نگاہوں کا جادو (the magic of my gaze) implies the lover's own sight is overpowered and bows in submission — a classical Urdu trope of the beloved's supremacy over the lover's perception; 'makes my sight bow low' partially captures this but loses the involuntary surrender.

metaphor_spans.abstract_meaning: the beloved's face as the moon — source of all light against which the world's beauty is measured
the beloved's eyes as a spell that disarms the lover's own power of sight
the lover's gaze rendered helpless and bowing before the beloved's radiance

source_lines: پھر بھی مجھے تیرے چہرے کی روشنی میں سجدہ ہے
translated_lines: I see the colors of the world,

stanzas.loss_note: سجدہ (sajda, prostration in prayer) is a precise Islamic devotional act — bowing the forehead to the ground before God. Its use here for the beloved's face is a classical Urdu convention of transferring divine worship to the beloved (a Sufi register); 'bow' in the translation loses this sacred-profane charge.

stanzas.loss_note: The source says the sorrow of passing moments also exists (ہوتا ہے) within the heartbeat even while smiling — a coexistence of grief and joy. The translation converts this into a simple transformation ('becomes a joy'), erasing the simultaneous duality that is the stanza's emotional point.
